transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Sierra Retail - Lead Eng), Ben Cole (CTO), Marta Ruiz (DevOps)

Summary:
Quick SDK (Python + TypeScript) walkthrough for Sierra Retail's engineering team. Focus on auth (API key vs. SSO for Console), environment setup, sample quickstarts, and next steps for a POC. Talked about Dedicated vs Hosted briefly for latency/cost tradeoffs. Agreed to share quickstart repo, security docs, and schedule pilot kickoff.

Topics covered:
- SDK install and quickstart (pip/npm)
- Auth options: api key, org keys, environment variables, KMS integration
- Running a local quickstart (Python example) and a TS example for serverless
- Console walkthrough: routes, keys, model selection, streaming
- Redwood Optimize mention: batching and quantization recommendations
- POC run criteria and baseline benchmarks

Transcript:
[00:00] Jenna Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jenna, AE at Redwood Inference, with Marco, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Aisha Khan: Doing good, thanks. We're excited to see the SDK flow and get the auth cleared up.
[00:12] Ben Cole: Yep, want to make sure we can onboard devs quickly, and Marta's here for infra questions.
[00:18] Marco Diaz: Great — we'll start with a short demo of the SDKs, then show the Console, and end with POC next steps. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:25] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. Quick note: we run in AWS us-west-2 and have strict KMS policies.
[00:30] Marco Diaz: Perfect, we'll cover KMS and VPC options in the security section.
[00:35] Jenna Park: Okay, first up SDKs. Marco, want to share your screen?
[00:40] Marco Diaz: Sure. (screen sharing) Alright, so here's our GitHub quickstart. We provide both Python and TypeScript examples. For Python it's pip install redwood-inference-sdk (note: package name in repo is redwood-sdk, sometimes the pip artifact differs).
[00:55] Marco Diaz: Example quickstart: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, then from redwood import Client; client = Client(); resp = client.generate(model="redwood-1-small", prompt="Summarize this order...") — simple as that.
[01:10] Aisha Khan: Quick question, does the SDK auto-retry on transient errors?
[01:14] Marco Diaz: Yes, the SDK has built-in retry/backoff and circuit-breaker hooks you can configure. Defaults are conservative.
[01:20] Ben Cole: How do we handle long-running prompts and streaming?
[01:24] Marco Diaz: For streaming we use the stream() method or the async iterator in Python. In TS we expose a readable stream you can pipe to SSE or websockets. There are examples in the quickstart.
[01:35] Marta Ruiz: About auth — we prefer not to store long-lived keys in code. Best practice?
[01:40] Jenna Park: We recommend storing keys in environment variables and using your cloud KMS to rotate them. For Dedicated/private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM. We also support short-lived tokens via our Console for CI workflows.
[01:55] Aisha Khan: Can you do SSO for Console access? We want RBAC for routes.
[01:59] Marco Diaz: Yes, Console supports SSO via SAML/Okta with role-based permissions. You can restrict keys to specific routes/models.
[02:06] Ben Cole: Any differences in the SDK when you run against Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted?
[02:10] Marco Diaz: Only the endpoint URL and key. With Dedicated you'll get a VPC hostname and a different token. SDK config supports passing explicit base_url and org_id. Note: sometimes SDK autoconfig tries hosted by default so set the env var REDWOOD_BASE_URL for Dedicated.
[02:25] Aisha Khan: Onboarding — how long to get a dev up and running?
[02:29] Jenna Park: Typically 30–60 minutes for basic generate/embed calls and a day to wire in streaming and production env. For the POC we'll give a step-by-step.
[02:36] Marco Diaz: I'll demo the Python quickstart now — running locally using a virtualenv.
[02:40] [02:40] Marco Diaz: (typing) python -m venv venv; source venv/bin/activate; pip install redwood-inference-sdk
[02:46] [02:46] Marco Diaz: Set export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx; python quickstart.py — this will call the hosted endpoint by default and print a generated summary.
[02:55] Aisha Khan: Are there rate limits on the hosted API we need to be aware of?
[02:59] Marco Diaz: Yes, by default there are per-account rate limits, but for pilots we can open limits. For Dedicated you get predictable throughput tied to reserved GPU pools.
[03:10] Ben Cole: We have heavy peak traffic on Black Friday equivalents; how does batching help?
[03:14] Marco Diaz: Redwood Optimize suggests batching configs and KV caching to reduce per-token cost while meeting latency SLOs. We can run a sample workload to recommend batch sizes.
[03:24] Marta Ruiz: For our infra, we prefer IaC. Anything to automate key rotation and environment setup?
[03:29] Marco Diaz: Yes, we provide terraform modules for dedicated and a small cloud-init script for hosted API environment variables. We'll share the repo.
[03:36] Aisha Khan: Show us a TypeScript serverless example? That's our primary stack for edge.
[03:40] Marco Diaz: Sure — npm i @redwood/inference (note: package naming varies in early docs). Then in Node/TS const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const stream = await client.streamGenerate({ model: 'redwood-chat-1', messages: [...] }); stream.on('data', chunk => {/* pipe to client */});
[03:58] Ben Cole: The TS quickstart mentions WebSocket keepalive — is that necessary for streaming?
[04:03] Marco Diaz: For long streams yes, we recommend a ping every 30s. The SDK handles this automatically unless you override low-level transport.
[04:10] Marta Ruiz: Any gotchas with Node v18 vs v20?
[04:13] Marco Diaz: We test v16–v20; if you use experimental fetch in v18 be careful with global fetch polyfills. We'll note recommended runtimes in the README.
[04:22] Aisha Khan: About logs and observability — do we get token-level cost breakdowns?
[04:26] Jenna Park: Console shows token-level cost, latency, and per-route dashboards. You can also export traces to your observability stack via hooks.
[04:33] Marco Diaz: (navigates Console) Here is the API keys page, model catalog, and route configuration. You can pin model versions and configure canary rollouts.
[04:45] [04:45] Marco Diaz: If you look under Routes, you can set batching policies and KV cache TTL per route. That's how you control latency vs cost trade-offs.
[04:56] Ben Cole: Security — is there an audit log for who called what?
[05:00] Marco Diaz: Yes, both Hosted and Dedicated offer audit logs. For Private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM and we support S3/GCS sinks.
[05:08] Marta Ruiz: For encryption at rest, do you manage keys in Hosted?
[05:11] Jenna Park: Hosted uses our managed keys by default, but you can bring your own KMS for Dedicated/Private. We support AWS KMS and customer HSM integrations.
[05:20] Aisha Khan: What about PII/data retention?
[05:23] Jenna Park: We have configurable retention policies; default is short retention and you can opt-out of training data usage. We'll share the data handling policy.
[05:33] Marco Diaz: Quick demo of a small benchmark script — this will run 100 short prompts and report median latency and tokens per second. (runs) Median 120ms per call on redwood-1-small for these short prompts, cost estimate shown.
[05:50] Ben Cole: Good to know. For the POC we want an apples-to-apples comparison vs our current OpenAI baseline. Can you share scripts?
[05:55] Marco Diaz: Yes, we'll include benchmark scripts that call both providers and output comparable metrics.
[06:02] Aisha Khan: About onboarding timeline — ideally pilot starts in two weeks. Is that doable?
[06:06] Jenna Park: Yes, we can kick off the week of 2026-07-12. We'll provide the quickstart repo and a checklist for infra.
[06:12] Marco Diaz: For pilot environment we'll need access to a staging cluster or a small test account; if you prefer we can provide a sandbox hosted account.
[06:20] Marta Ruiz: We prefer sandbox hosted first while we vet security, then Dedicated later.
[06:25] Jenna Park: That's a common path. We'll send sandbox creds and a step-by-step to run the quickstarts.
[06:31] Ben Cole: One more on pricing — do you have committed pricing for Dedicated?
[06:35] Jenna Park: Yes, Dedicated is reservation-based with monthly/annual commits. I'll include pricing ranges in the deck. For hosted API we have per-token pricing and pilot credits.
[06:45] Aisha Khan: Any limitation on model weights we can bring? We plan to test an internal finetuned model.
[06:50] Marco Diaz: You can host private models on Dedicated/Private; for hosted we support vetted models from our catalog. For private model hosting we work with you on onboarding and kernel selection.
[07:00] (brief crosstalk)
[07:05] Jenna Park: Okay, recap and next steps — we'll: 1) Share quickstart repo with Python and TS examples, 2) Send security and SOC2 docs, 3) Share benchmark scripts and sample env templates, 4) Schedule POC kickoff week of 7/12. Anything to add?
[07:20] Aisha Khan: Please add a short checklist for infra requirements for sandbox vs dedicated.
[07:26] Marco Diaz: Will do. I'll also include sample terraform snippets for KMS and route setup.
[07:33] Ben Cole: Good. Also add expected SLAs for Dedicated in the deck.
[07:38] Jenna Park: Will add that.
[07:40] Marta Ruiz: Thanks — otherwise this was very helpful.
[07:42] Jenna Park: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up with the items.
[07:46] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quality: Some product names were slightly mis-transcribed (package names and npm/pip artifacts). Repo and package names to be verified in the materials we send.
